To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

NPT2a knockout mice respond differently to changes in dietary calcium and phosphate than do wild-type mice, that the response of Npt2 knockout mice to dietary phosphate is blunted, and that the urinary calcium x phosphate product and plasma phosphate levels are positively correlated to renal phosphate deposits while urine phosphate and the urine anions gap are negatively correlated.
Npt2a(-/-) mice develop hypercalciuria and hyperphosphatemia in the presence of normal plasma 1,25(OH)2D levels, and the response of PTH levels to dietary phosphate is blunted when compared with WT.
Npt2a deficiency leads to renal calcium phosphate deposits that are exacerbated by phosphate and calcium in the diet and that the response to dietary phosphate of PTH and FGF23 is blunted.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the pathophysiology of calcium and phosphate homeostasis in patients with mutations in NPT2a or NPT2c and with the potential development of therapies for these patients.

the pathogenesis of calcium phosphate deposits in the kidney.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the NPT2a-/- mouse is a model of hypercalciuric nephrocalcinotic renal disease that responds to dietary calcium and phosphate and that the response of this model to dietary calcium and calcium and phosphate is different from that of wild type mice.
NPT2a-/- are a good model of human renal stone disease and may help in the development of novel therapeutics.

Npt2 knockout mice respond differently to calcium, phosphate and PTH when compared to wild type mice, which in turn suggests that the NPT2 knockout mice are a good animal model to study the pathogenesis and treatment of renal stone disease in humans.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Npt2 knockout mice have a blunted response to dietary phosphate and a blunted response of PTH and FGF23 to dietary phosphate.
NPT2a-/- and Npt2c-/- mice have a different response to dietary calcium and phosphate than WT mice and that the urinary calcium excretion is the major determinant of renal calcium phosphate deposits.
Npt2 knockout mice respond differently to the addition of dietary phosphate than wildtype mice.
The main takeaway from our work is that
dietary phosphate and calcium have a profound effect on the formation of renal phosphate deposits in NPT2a knockout mice.
the response to dietary phosphate and calcium of NPT2 knockout mice is different from wild-type mice and this may be clinically important.

Npt2A-/- mice respond to dietary phosphate differently than WT mice and the relative contribution of dietary calcium, phosphate, PTH and urinary anion gap to the formation of calcium phosphate deposits in the kidney may be different in Npt2A-deficient mice than in WT mice.
